records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: What LLDP-MED actually negotiates LLDP advertises device identity and capabilities over Layer 2. LLDP-MED extends it for media endpoints such as IP phones. Its network-policy TLV can advertise the voice VLAN, Layer-2 priority, and DSCP values; other TLVs provide location identification and inventory details, and LLDP can also expose PoE capabilities. The switch is not simply “putting the phone in a VLAN” by itself: it is advertising a policy that a capable phone may use to tag its voice traffic. For a phone and PC sharing a switch port, the common design keeps the PC on the native/data VLAN while the phone tags voice traffic into a separate voice VLAN. The LLDP profile must advertise the correct voice VLAN policy, and the port must actually carry that VLAN. A profile that references a nonexistent VLAN interface, is not assigned to the port, or is not transmitted because LLDP is disabled cannot produce the intended result. Configuration relationships On a FortiGate-managed FortiSwitch, the LLDP profile is configured under the switch-controller LLDP profile hierarchy; standalone FortiSwitch uses its own switch LLDP profile hierarchy. records.lesson_subject: Wireless client load balancing: AP handoff versus frequency handoff and RSSI-driven retries
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: wireless-client-load-balancing-ap-handoff-versus-frequency-handoff-and-rssi-driven-retries
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Two different steering mechanisms FortiGate wireless controllers support access-point handoff and frequency handoff. AP handoff addresses an overloaded AP: if the station count crosses a configured threshold, the controller can signal a weak client to move to a nearby AP that can hear it adequately. When a new client joins while several APs are busy, the controller can select a less-loaded nearby AP to respond. Frequency handoff encourages dual-band clients to use 5 GHz when their measured signal is strong enough, leaving more 2.4 GHz airtime for devices that need it. These are controller-driven association behaviors, not an instruction that forcibly moves every client at any time. Wi-Fi clients make the final association decisions and can ignore or retry a steer. The controller may withhold a response on 2.4 GHz to encourage a capable client to retry on 5 GHz. If 5 GHz signal quality is actually inadequate, the client may retry or fall back. Roaming clients are excluded from the documented load-balancing behavior, so do not use this feature as a universal roaming fix. records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: A rule is a query plus grouping, threshold, and incident semantics FortiSIEM rule conditions are built from event filters and one or more subpatterns. Group-by attributes define which events belong to the same logical group; aggregate conditions define the threshold that triggers an incident. For example, COUNT(Matched Events) >= 10 with no group-by aggregates matching events together, while grouping by Source IP creates separate threshold calculations per source. Purpose and object model A FortiManager firmware template expresses desired firmware state for FortiGate and managed access devices such as FortiAP, FortiSwitch, and FortiExtender. The template can be assigned to one or more devices, with either a scheduled campaign or a manually initiated upgrade. Purpose and control model Distributed Automatic Radio Resource Provisioning (DARRP) lets managed FortiAP radios choose operating channels from RF measurements rather than relying only on a static channel plan. Why secure/static ports exist FortiNAC can disable an individual host by physical address when a shared switch port serves multiple endpoints or a Dead End VLAN is unavailable. On supported switches, a secure/static port acts as the restricted port for disabled MAC addresses. When FortiNAC disables a host manually or through an alarm action, it sends the device a message that places that MAC in the device's restricted list. The disabled MAC is then permitted only on the designated secure/static port; if it appears on another port, the switch blocks its access. The secure port itself is a security boundary. It must not be connected to an ordinary production endpoint or an unrestricted access segment. If a disabled host is plugged into the secure port, the mechanism can intentionally permit access there, defeating the containment design. Collection architecture Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) is a Windows-native aggregation path. Source computers forward selected event channels to a Windows Event Collector (WEC); the WEC stores them in its ForwardedEvents log. FortiSIEM's Windows Agent is installed on the WEC host and reads that consolidated log. This reduces the number of FortiSIEM agents, but changes what the collector sees as the transport source. Two steering models, one flow FortiSASE can steer browser traffic through an agentless explicit-proxy/PAC path or through an agent-based Secure Internet Access (SIA) tunnel. They are different access models. The explicit proxy terminates the browser's proxy connection at the FortiSASE proxy service (default port 9443) and applies web policy there. The SIA tunnel encapsulates endpoint traffic into the managed tunnel path. They should not both steer the same browser flow. Why the 403 occurs The October 6, 2026 Community troubleshooting tip describes a 403 domain-fronting blocked response when the proxy and SIA tunnel are active together. The proxy service changes the Server Name Indication (SNI). When the already-proxied traffic then reaches FortiSASE through the SIA tunnel, the SNI and tunnel path conflict with the expected domain identity, so FortiSASE blocks the request. records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: ldap-authentication-cache-two-minute-successful-authentication-reuse-imported-user-dependency-and-revocation-t | cache scope and purpose / transaction behavior / verification and fault isolation

Cache scope and purpose FortiAuthenticator’s documented LDAP authentication cache reduces repeated calls to a remote directory. Remote LDAP users must be imported into the FortiAuthenticator user database. After an LDAP user authenticates successfully, subsequent authentication requests from the same user within a two-minute window can succeed without another check against the remote LDAP server. This is a short successful-authentication cache, not a replacement for LDAP user import, directory synchronization, or the remote directory’s identity store. Transaction behavior On a cache miss, FortiAuthenticator must perform the remote LDAP authentication path. If that succeeds, the successful result can be reused for the same user during the documented two-minute window. Repeated requests in that interval therefore may not create a matching bind/authentication event on the LDAP server. A cache hit proves FortiAuthenticator has a recent successful result for that use

FEC protects a tunnel flow from loss Forward Error Correction sends redundant packets so the receiver can reconstruct some lost data without waiting for retransmission. Fortinet describes a base/redundant relationship: x redundant packets are sent for every y base packets. Adaptive FEC changes that ratio as SD-WAN SLA measurements change. records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Editable draw.io Standalone SVG A static virtual IP (VIP) is a destination-NAT object. It tells FortiOS that traffic addressed to an external address (or address/port tuple) should be translated to an internal server address. A one-to-one VIP maps the full port range; a port-forwarding VIP narrows the translation to selected external and mapped ports. The VIP is not itself an allow rule: the forwarded flow still needs a firewall policy whose destination references the VIP. Objects and packet transaction Keep four values separate: extip is the public address clients target; extintf constrains the interface on which the VIP is valid; mappedip is the real server address; and, for port forwarding, extport / mappedport describe the service translation. The ingress packet first matches the VIP translation. FortiGate then evaluates the forwarding policy using the VIP object as the destination, checks the service/source/schedule and route, and forwards toward the mapped server. The server's return traffic must route back through the FortiGate so reverse translation can be applied to the session. Central NAT changes where DNAT objects are managed in the GUI: use Policy & Objects > DNAT & Virtual IPs instead of the ordinary Virtual IPs page. It does not make the VIP object a substitute for a firewall policy. Configuration sketch config firewall vip edit "Web_HTTPS" set extip 203.0.113

records.lesson_subject: Normalized interfaces with per-device and per-platform mapping
records.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: normalized-interfaces-with-per-device-and-per-platform-mapping | two mapping scopes, one policy reference / configuration workflow / cli representation and boundaries / verification and troubleshooting
records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Editable draw.io Standalone SVG Normalized interfaces let one ADOM policy refer to a logical interface name even when managed FortiGates use different physical ports or device zones. The object is a translation layer in FortiManager's policy database; it is not a new interface created on the FortiGate. At installation time, FortiManager resolves the logical name into the target device's real interface. Two mapping scopes, one policy reference A per-platform mapping associates a normalized interface with an interface name for a model family. It is useful when a set of same-model devices share a port layout. A per-device mapping binds the logical name to the interface or zone on one specific managed device/VDOM. When both mappings exist, the per-device value is the more specific override; devices without a matching device entry use the applicable platform/default mapping. If neither mapping resolves, install compilation can fail with a missing or undefined dynamic interface. For example, the shared policy can use VOICE as its incoming interface. records.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: 527 focused lesson words Bonjour is service discovery, not ordinary unicast routing Bonjour uses multicast DNS (mDNS) and DNS-based service discovery so clients can find services such as printers, AirPlay receivers and casting devices without a conventional DNS server entry. In a segmented enterprise WLAN, the multicast discovery packets normally remain within their Layer-2/VLAN scope. A Bonjour profile lets the FortiAP WLAN system selectively advertise chosen services from one VLAN into another. It is not a general-purpose bridge between VLANs: the profile's source VLAN, destination VLAN and service list define what is exposed. Profile objects and precedence A Bonjour profile contains a policy list. Each policy entry identifies the source VLAN with from-vlan , the destination VLAN with to-vlan , and the service types to advertise. The profile can be applied to a FortiAP profile or directly to a device. If both levels contain a Bonjour profile, the device-level configuration takes precedence. That precedence is important during troubleshooting: editing the AP profile will not change behavior on an AP that has a device-level override. config wireless-controller bonjour-profile edit "floor1-services" set micro-location enable config policy-list edit 1 set from-vlan "100" set to-vlan "200" set services airplay printers chromecast next end next end config wireless-controller wtp-pr

Inline-CASB places application-aware controls in the traffic path between a remote user and a SaaS provider. It differs from an API-based CASB that queries a cloud service out of band. FortiSASE uses IPS protocol decoders to recognize application traffic, including traffic on non-standard ports, and supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 detection. SSL deep inspection exposes HTTPS content so the platform can identify the SaaS application and, with Web Filter Inline-CASB, modify HTTP headers used by the provider for tenant restrictions. Two related but distinct controls. Application Control With Inline-CASB applies category-level actions: Allow, Monitor or Block. Allow passes traffic to web filtering, antivirus and DLP inspection. Monitor processes the traffic like Allow but logs each matching pattern. Block denies attempts to access applications in the category. Application Overrides can set an individual application to a different action than its category. Separately, Web Filter with Inline-CASB can insert or remove HTTP headers on matching SaaS requests/responses. Category control decides whether an application is permitted; header insertion can constrain which tenant or organization the user may access within an otherwise allowed application. Open standalone SVG · Open editable draw.io source Threat model and evaluation IPv6 Router Advertisements (RAs) are ICMPv6 messages by which routers advertise default-router information and prefix/configuration parameters to neighboring hosts. A rogue RA on an access VLAN can redirect hosts toward an unauthorized router or advertise incorrect IPv6 configuration. FortiSwitch RA Guard evaluates each RA against a policy before forwarding it. The documented criteria include the Managed (M) and Other (O) flags, minimum and maximum hop limit, maximum router preference, allowed source IPv6 address, allowed advertised prefix, and whether the device is treated as a host or router. If the device role is host, all RAs are dropped. If it is router, the remaining criteria are evaluated. This makes the role assignment a security boundary: apply router-role policies only where a legitimate router is expected. A model is the algorithm for a specific task, such as login anomaly or traffic download anomaly. An asset is the entity being monitored, such as an end user or endpoint. candidate_selection.lesson_subject: FortiAnalyzer forwarding-mode log export: reliable TCP buffering, filters, exclusions and masking
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: client-side forwarding profile -> destination type FAZ/syslog/CEF/output plugin -> device/log filters and field exclusions/masking -> TCP reliable buffer or UDP -> remote receiver
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: create forwarding entry on source FortiAnalyzer; select server type and destination; optionally filter devices/logs and mask fields; enable reliable TCP; forward real-time or near-real-time; remote FAZ authorizes forwarded devices
candidate_selection.failure_class: transport UDP loss; TCP buffer saturation; unsupported server type/port; filters suppress needed events; remote device remains unauthorized
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: get system log-forward; forwarding status; remote connection; sender buffer/backlog; receiver device authorization and incoming log timestamps
candidate_selection.remediation_path: separate forwarding from aggregation mode; confirm destination protocol and port; use reliable TCP where supported; verify filter logic and masking; authorize remote FAZ devices; check buffer headroom
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: distinguish real-time forwarding from scheduled FAZ aggregation and determine why logs are delayed, filtered or held in buffer
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: source FAZ log stream -> forwarding profile/filter/mask -> TCP/UDP transport -> remote FAZ/syslog/CEF receiver

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: LACP trunk formation and member-selection behavior: aggregator mode, fallback and hash fields
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: config switch trunk -> LACP active/passive or static/fortinet-trunk mode -> aggregator selection by bandwidth/count -> per-flow port-selection criteria -> optional fallback-port and member withdrawal behavior
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: define trunk members and mode; negotiate LACP if active/passive; select eligible aggregator; hash source/destination MAC/IP to member; handle partner absence via fallback or member withdrawal policy
candidate_selection.failure_class: partner not negotiating; mismatched LACP mode/key; fallback hides peer misconfiguration; poor hash entropy causes uneven utilization; member withdrawal blocks traffic
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: show switch trunk; LACP actor/partner state; per-member counters; port-selection criteria; link state and fallback member
candidate_selection.remediation_path: match LACP settings at both ends; verify actor/partner state; choose hash tuple that fits traffic diversity; configure fallback only for intentional non-LACP peer; validate min/max bundle and withdrawal behavior
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: distinguish a formed LACP bundle from balanced traffic distribution and predict which flow tuple keeps traffic on one member
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: two peer switches -> LACP control exchange -> aggregator selection -> flow hash -> individual trunk member links

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: SSID VLAN pooling: AP-group assignment versus tunnel-mode client load balancing
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: SSID VAP VLAN pool -> optional AP-group-to-VLAN mapping or tunnel-mode client load balancer -> round-robin least-populated VLAN or hash selection -> generated SSID zone
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: define VLAN pool under VAP; create matching VLAN interfaces/networks/DHCP; choose wtp-group, round-robin or hash; AP association selects VLAN; client obtains address from selected VLAN
candidate_selection.failure_class: pool VLAN has no valid member; VLAN interface/DHCP missing; attempt to use load balancing in bridge mode; mistaken assumption hash and round-robin are equivalent
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: show wireless-controller vap; SSID zone membership; client association VLAN; DHCP lease and VLAN interface counters
candidate_selection.remediation_path: verify every pool VLAN is valid and provisioned; use tunnel mode for load-balancing pools; distinguish AP-group mapping from client-count balancing; confirm DHCP and policy for each VLAN
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: choose the right pool method for per-AP segmentation versus client load distribution and identify fallback to static VLAN
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: SSID VAP -> VLAN pool selector (AP group/round-robin/hash) -> SSID zone/VLAN interfaces -> DHCP scopes -> wireless clients

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: FortiNAC 9.4 Kerberos authentication enablement for administrators and users: separate Winbind and LDAP dependencies
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiNAC 9.4 Kerberos authentication capability for CA admin/user login and FortiNAC Manager admin login, distinct from LDAP directory synchronization and Winbind MSCHAPv2 RADIUS path
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: configure directory/realm identity and Kerberos prerequisites; authenticate administrator or portal user using Kerberos; keep LDAP sync and RADIUS MSCHAPv2 Winbind as separate functions; verify role mapping and service-specific login
candidate_selection.failure_class: Kerberos realm/NetBIOS mismatch; DNS SRV lookup or time skew; confusing LDAP bind success with Kerberos ticket authentication; unsupported authentication plane
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: FortiNAC authentication logs; Kerberos/Winbind service status; DNS SRV lookup; NTP offset; LDAP user lookup versus actual GUI login result
candidate_selection.remediation_path: verify DNS and _kerberos/_ldap SRV records; align realm and NetBIOS values; synchronize NTP; validate which login plane is in use; avoid joining non-AD LDAP/Kerberos directories through Samba Winbind
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: separate FortiNAC 9.4 Kerberos login capability from LDAP directory sync and Winbind-based PEAP/MSCHAPv2 authentication
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiNAC CA/Manager login -> Kerberos KDC ticket path; parallel LDAP directory sync and Winbind RADIUS path kept separate

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: IP phone voice VLAN provisioning: Local RADIUS attributes and MAC-notification-driven refresh
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: IP-phone host profile -> Network Access Policy -> Logical Network -> Local RADIUS attribute group (Tunnel-Medium-Type, Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Private-Group-Id, Cisco-AVPair voice class) -> switch tagged voice VLAN
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: phone is profiled/registered; FortiNAC selects voice policy; RADIUS Access-Accept returns VLAN and voice attributes; switch places phone in voice VLAN; MAC notification traps can trigger revalidation on connect/disconnect
candidate_selection.failure_class: Local versus Proxy RADIUS mode confusion; missing policy; mismatched RADIUS shared secret; incorrect VLAN attribute group; noisy MAC notification traps
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: RADIUS Access-Request/Accept attributes; switch port voice/data VLAN state; FortiNAC host profile/policy; MAC notification trap event timeline
candidate_selection.remediation_path: confirm Local RADIUS requirement; create profile/policy/logical network; use RFC VLAN attributes plus Cisco-AVPair; match shared secret; enable MAC traps only when real-time voice provisioning is required
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: diagnose why an IP phone receives data VLAN but not voice VLAN by separating policy match, RADIUS attribute response and switch interpretation
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: IP phone -> access switch -> RADIUS Access-Request -> FortiNAC policy/attribute group -> Access-Accept -> tagged voice VLAN

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: Self-service password recovery with SMS or FortiToken verification and rate-limited portal workflow
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Authentication portal pre-login Password Reset option -> permitted verification methods -> per-user SMS/FortiToken recovery enrollment -> rate-limited recovery transaction -> LDAP/local password update
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: enable Password Reset and select verification methods in portal policy; configure user recovery options or LDAP sync rule; user requests reset; proves identity by SMS or FortiToken; reset operation updates account password
candidate_selection.failure_class: portal method disabled; user lacks recovery channel; SMS gateway or token delivery failure; LDAP permission/LDAPS constraint; rate limit reached
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: portal pre-login configuration; user recovery options; SMS/token send and verification logs; LDAP bind/reset permissions; rate-limit response
candidate_selection.remediation_path: enable supported method in portal; provision user or remote LDAP sync recovery options; verify SMS delivery and FortiToken enrollment; confirm LDAPS/domain-join permissions; respect throttling before retry
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: distinguish portal-wide verification methods from per-user recovery enrollment and identify why a user sees no SMS or token option
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: user portal reset request -> selected SMS/FortiToken factor -> recovery verification -> local/LDAP password update

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: Native RDP TCP forwarding mode: transport fallback and lost native RDP security controls
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: RDP Service secret -> TCP Forwarding option -> FortiPAM TCP tunnel consistent with Other clientType launcher instead of native RDP launcher integration
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: enable TCP forwarding for RDP secret; client establishes forwarded TCP path through FortiPAM; remote endpoint receives RDP stream; certificate revocation or legacy RDP protocol issue bypassed at the native launcher layer
candidate_selection.failure_class: native RDP launch fails certificate revocation check or protocol compatibility; operator enables TCP forwarding but assumes native RDP features still apply
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: secret RDP Service configuration; launcher/client type; TCP forwarding session state; observed absence of RDP security level, Restricted Admin, Auto TOTP and clipboard block controls
candidate_selection.remediation_path: use TCP forwarding only for documented compatibility reasons; if native RDP controls are required, keep TCP forwarding disabled and fix certificate/protocol prerequisites; test with least privilege
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: select TCP forwarding to bypass native-launch compatibility failure while recognizing which native RDP security features are no longer available
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiPAM RDP secret -> TCP forwarding tunnel -> target RDP service; native RDP feature-control branch omitted

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: FortiSIEM discovery orchestration: Range Scan, Smart Scan, cloud scans and Collector/Worker job placement
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: discovery entry type/range/root IP -> credential mapping -> Collector performs discovery when assigned; otherwise Supervisor discovers and distributes performance jobs to active Workers via weighted round robin
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: create discovery range and include/exclude criteria; map credentials by device type/domain; run or schedule scan; Collector/Supervisor discovers and returns CMDB objects; inspect results/errors/changes and assign ongoing monitoring jobs
candidate_selection.failure_class: wrong scan type/root IP; credential mapping absent or ambiguous; scan scope too broad; ping precheck suppresses non-ICMP hosts; Worker reassignment changes monitoring placement
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: discovery Results/Errors/History/Changes; Collector assignment; CMDB host inventory; credential test; job distribution status
candidate_selection.remediation_path: select Range/Smart/L2/cloud scan appropriately; validate credentials and IP-to-credential mapping; use do-not-ping option where required; narrow include/exclude; schedule off-peak and inspect changes/errors
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: distinguish Smart Scan topology traversal from Range Scan and diagnose why a Collector discovery result does not imply monitoring jobs are on the Supervisor
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: discovery definition -> Collector or Supervisor -> discovered devices/CMDB -> Worker performance-monitoring job assignment

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: FortiSASE external log forwarding: server access type, reliable TCP and TLS trust chain
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Security PoP logs -> external server profile -> Public/Private reachability via internet or SPA FortiGate hub -> FAZ/syslog/CEF destination -> reliable TCP and optional TLS CA validation
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: enable external log forwarding; select server type and public/private access; define endpoint and port; choose forwarding frequency; for syslog enable reliable TCP and secure TLS; upload remote CA; verify Connecting to Connected
candidate_selection.failure_class: private server lacks SPA path; primary/secondary access-type constraint; TLS fails because remote CA missing; UDP/TCP reachability or cipher incompatibility
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: FortiSASE connection status; selected access type; remote server listener; TLS certificate chain and CA; receiver log timestamps and per-log-type arrival
candidate_selection.remediation_path: match Public/Private to actual route; ensure SPA hub for private endpoint; import remote CA; use TCP for reliable delivery; validate server port/ciphers and allowed log types
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: distinguish a network reachability failure from TLS trust failure and select the correct Public/Private server path
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiSASE Security PoP log sources -> forwarding profile -> public internet or SPA hub -> FAZ/syslog/CEF collector

candidate_selection.lesson_subject: Passive application-specific SLA measurement: per-service latency/jitter/loss from inspected live sessions
candidate_selection.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: firewall policy passive-wan-health-measurement + application-control identification + passive/prefer-passive performance SLA + SD-WAN service passive-measurement per ISDB/application
candidate_selection.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: enable passive measurements on policy and SD-WAN rule; classify traffic by ISDB/application signatures; collect live session metrics by application and member; compare SLA thresholds; steer subsequent flows based on per-application measured path quality
candidate_selection.failure_class: hardware offload left enabled; application classification missing; no live traffic for passive-only SLA; using active probe metrics as proxy for application performance
candidate_selection.evidence_pattern: diagnose sys link-monitor-passive admin list by-interface; per-rule SLA metrics; policy application-control profile; passive-measurement setting; interface session samples
candidate_selection.remediation_path: disable auto-asic-offload on participating policies; enable app-control classification; use passive or prefer-passive health check; generate representative app traffic; use active fallback where idle paths need measurement
candidate_selection.question_fingerprint: explain why a generic ping SLA is healthy while one application has poor latency and identify the policy/rule requirements for per-application passive measurement
candidate_selection.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: application session -> firewall policy inspection -> passive metrics collector -> app-specific SLA per WAN member -> SD-WAN rule steering
